searchText: > Another question: I would love to be able to run one instance of each popular ethereum client, like geth, open ethereum, besu, etc. However, as each client stores the state in its own different way, each one needs to have a seperate copy of the ethereum state. I guess there's no way to avoid this but wondering if once a chain is downloaded by one client if it can be transformed to the format expected by the other clients? And if that might be a project worth pursuing? <@!387536747476549632> I'm a bit late on this, but I have a branch of py-evm which can read from Geth's database format, so you can use Trinity against a Geth database. I also have a script which goes a step further and imports a geth database, turning it into a database which Trinity can run against. One problem with the idea is that importing a Geth database into TurboGeth is going to take a very long time, and It would probably take a lot of effort to make a version of TurboGeth which can operate against a Geth database, it almost ruins the point of using TurboGeth 🙂 <timbeiko> > if once a chain is downloaded by one client if it can be transformed to the format expected by the other clients? And if that might be a project worth pursuing? You can do this with the chain data on a few clients. I know you can import geth blocks in besu, for instance, but it still means you need to run two full databases. The only saving is that if you already have a geth node you can export from, you don’t need get all the blocks from the network directly. > It would probably take a lot of effort to make a version of TurboGeth which can operate against a Geth database, it almost ruins the point of using TurboGeth 🙂 <@!296630428754771968> That is definitely true

excerpts.content:
> Another question: I would love to be able to run one instance of each popular ethereum client, like geth, open ethereum, besu, etc. However, as each client stores the state in its own different way, each one needs to have a seperate copy of the ethereum state. I guess there's no way to avoid this but wondering if once a chain is downloaded by one client if it can be transformed to the format expected by the other clients? And if that might be a project worth pursuing?
<@!387536747476549632> I'm a bit late on this, but I have a branch of py-evm which can read from Geth's database format, so you can use Trinity against a Geth database. I also have a script which goes a step further and imports a geth database, turning it into a database which Trinity can run against. One problem with the idea is that importing a Geth database into TurboGeth is going to take a very long time, and It would probably take a lot of effort to make a version of TurboGeth which can operate against a Geth database, it almost ruins the point of using TurboGeth 🙂

excerpts.author: eth2_gitter_bot
excerpts.content:
<timbeiko> > if once a chain is downloaded by one client if it can be transformed to the format expected by the other clients? And if that might be a project worth pursuing?
You can do this with the chain data on a few clients. I know you can import geth blocks in besu, for instance, but it still means you need to run two full databases. The only saving is that if you already have a geth node you can export from, you don’t need get all the blocks from the network directly.
